η = Φ ÷ P, light output per watt, in lm/W

takeaways: A coil ignition makes high voltage only because the primary current is cut quickly: the collapsing flux induces a large emf in the many secondary turns, and the capacitor stops the points arcing so the collapse is fast.
Spark interval T<sub>s</sub> = 120 ÷ (N × z); with a fixed dwell angle the dwell time, coil current and spark energy all fall as speed rises.
The plug needs more voltage with a wider gap and a higher pressure, less with hot electrodes; the engine runs only while the coil's available voltage exceeds the plug's firing voltage.
Electronic ignition swaps the points for a pick-up and a transistor; constant-energy dwell keeps the coil current, and programmed ignition reads the advance from a speed-load map with corrections.
Waste spark fires a pair of plugs once per revolution with no cam sensor; direct ignition fires one coil per cylinder on compression and needs the cam sensor.
Compare light sources by efficacy (lm/W), colour, start-up time and life; light on the road follows E = I ÷ d².
Every lamp sits in a battery → fuse → switch or relay → lamp → earth circuit, in parallel with the others, with legal colours and a fuse sized to the wire.
Adaptive lighting levels the beam for pitch and swivels it for steering, with limits and safe fail modes.
The cluster is a bus node: speed comes from counted pulses, other readings from CAN frames and senders.
Wipers get two speeds from a third brush and stop through a cam park switch; the horn is a self-interrupting buzzer on a relay; the immobiliser, not the fob, decides whether the engine may start.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for labelled sketches with explanation: the coil ignition circuit, electronic and distributorless ignition, lamp circuits, the wiper motor with its park switch and the horn. Short calculations on spark interval, dwell, coil energy, lamp current and speedometer pulses are common, so carry the formulas in this book into the hall.

outline: Primary path: battery, switch, ballast, primary winding, contact breaker, earth
Current builds over the dwell and stores energy ½Li²
Points open: field collapses, emf induced in the many secondary turns
Capacitor stops arcing and speeds the collapse
Distributor routes the pulse to the plug in firing order; advance mechanisms

answer.text: Draw the circuit. The primary circuit runs battery → ignition switch → ballast resistor → coil primary → contact breaker → earth, with a capacitor across the points. The secondary circuit runs coil secondary → distributor rotor and cap → plug lead → plug → earth.

svg.aria: Battery-and-coil ignition circuit with ballast, points, capacitor, distributor and plug, and the dwell strip

answer: Name the parts and their jobs. The battery supplies 12 V; the ignition switch connects the system; the ballast resistor limits running current and is bypassed during cranking; the coil has a primary of a few hundred thick turns and a secondary of about 100 times as many fine turns on one iron core; the cam-driven points switch the primary; the capacitor (0.2–0.3 µF) sits across the points; the distributor routes each pulse to the plug in the firing order; the centrifugal and vacuum units move the timing.

Points closed (dwell). Current rises along i = (V/R)(1 − e<sup>−t/τ</sup>) with τ = L/R. For L = 8 mH and R = 3.0 Ω, τ = 2.67 ms and the final current is 12 ÷ 3.0 = 4.0 A. After a 6 ms dwell the current is 4.0 × (1 − e<sup>−2.25</sup>) = 3.58 A, and the core stores E = ½ × 0.008 × 3.58² = 51.2 mJ.

Points open (the break). The cam lifts the moving contact; the primary current falls to zero in a few microseconds and the flux collapses. By e = −N dΦ/dt an emf of a few hundred volts appears in the primary, and the secondary, with about 100 times the turns, gives roughly 100 × that, 10–25 kV or more.

Role of the capacitor. At the instant of opening the capacitor takes the primary current, so no arc forms between the separating contacts. The current therefore stops fast, dΦ/dt is large, the secondary voltage is high, and the points do not burn.

Breakdown and spark. The secondary voltage rises until the plug gap ionises (the firing voltage, about 10–20 kV), then falls to a spark-line voltage of 1–2 kV while the arc burns for 1–2 ms using the stored energy. The arc lights the compressed charge a little before TDC.

Distribution. The rotor, turning at half crank speed in a four-stroke engine, lines up with one cap segment at each break, so the pulse goes to the cylinder near the end of compression, in the order 1-3-4-2 on a typical four-cylinder engine.
Timing. Centrifugal weights advance the spark as speed rises; a vacuum diaphragm fed from a port above the throttle adds advance at part-throttle cruise. Total advance = base + centrifugal + vacuum.

bank.q: What decides the voltage needed to fire a spark plug? Explain the effect of electrode gap, compression pressure and electrode temperature, and why misfire appears first at high load.
outline: Breakdown needs a field strong enough to ionise the gap; define firing voltage
Wider gap: more voltage
Higher pressure: more voltage
Hot electrodes: less voltage; worn, rounded electrodes: more
Available voltage against required voltage: the reserve; high load uses it up
answer: Define the firing voltage. The gas in the gap is an insulator. When the voltage rises, the few free electrons are accelerated by the field and, if they gain enough energy between collisions, knock more electrons off gas molecules. The avalanche turns the gap into a conducting arc. The voltage at which this happens is the firing (breakdown) voltage V<sub>f</sub>.

Electrode gap. For a given voltage the field is E = V ÷ g, so a wider gap g needs a proportionally higher voltage to reach the same field. Worn plugs have wider gaps, so they need more voltage. For the example engine of the book, V<sub>f</sub> ≈ 10 + 22 g kV at full load.

Compression pressure. Denser gas means the electrons travel a shorter distance between collisions, so they need a stronger field to gain enough energy. Full load and high compression ratios raise the pressure at the spark, so V<sub>f</sub> rises. At light load the same engine needs only about 5 + 12 g kV.

Electrode temperature and shape. A hot surface frees electrons more easily, so V<sub>f</sub> falls as the electrodes heat up; a cold engine needs more voltage. Sharp edges concentrate the field and lower V<sub>f</sub>; worn, rounded electrodes raise it. Fouling deposits leak charge away before the voltage builds.
Mixture. A lean mixture needs a slightly higher voltage and a longer, stronger spark to light.

Pressure and gap together. For a uniform field the breakdown voltage depends on the product of pressure and gap (Paschen's law), which is why a plug that fires on the bench at 1 bar can still miss in the engine at 10–15 bar: the engine multiplies the pressure several times over.

Polarity. Coils are wired so the centre electrode is negative, because the hotter centre electrode gives off electrons more easily, which lowers the firing voltage; reversed coil leads raise the voltage the plug needs.

answer: The remedy is a smaller gap (25 = 10 + 22 g gives g = 0.68 mm), a higher-output coil, or fresh plugs, since wear raises V<sub>f</sub> further.
Check: the light-load reserve of 9.2 kV shrinks to a deficit of 4.8 kV, a swing of 14 kV caused only by load, which is why a weak ignition shows up as a misfire under hard acceleration.

bank.q: Explain how an electronic ignition system uses a pick-up and a switching transistor in place of contact-breaker points, and how constant-energy dwell control works.
outline: Problems of the points
Pick-up types: inductive, Hall effect
Igniter transistor switches the coil current
Constant dwell against constant energy with current limiting
Advantages
answer: State the problems of the points. They break a few amperes many times a second, so they burn; the rubbing block wears, so the dwell drifts; at high speed the fixed dwell angle gives too little charging time; and the contacts can bounce.

Pick-up (position sensor). An inductive pick-up has a permanent magnet and coil facing a toothed reluctor; each tooth changes the magnetic path and induces an alternating voltage whose size grows with speed. A Hall-effect pick-up has a Hall chip and magnet separated by a rotating vane; it gives a clean square wave whose size does not depend on speed, so it works down to cranking speed. Either gives one signal per cylinder per cycle at a known crank angle.

Igniter. The pick-up signal goes to the ignition module, which drives a power transistor (often a Darlington or IGBT) in series with the coil primary. Transistor on = current builds (dwell); transistor off = the break, and the coil fires exactly as with points. The pick-up only reports position; it carries no coil current.

Constant dwell. Early modules copied the points: the transistor conducts for a fixed fraction of each spark interval, so the dwell angle is fixed and the dwell time falls with speed. At 6000 rpm a 60% dwell on a four-cylinder engine gives only 0.60 × 5 ms = 3 ms.

Constant energy. A low-resistance, low-inductance coil reaches its current quickly. The module senses the primary current with a small resistor and switches on just early enough to reach a set current, say 7.5 A, before each spark; a current-limiting stage then holds 7.5 A until the break. It also lengthens the dwell when the battery voltage is low.

answer: Advantages: no burning or wear of contacts and no dwell drift; the same coil energy at all but the highest speeds; higher primary current possible, so higher secondary voltage and energy; accurate, maintenance-free timing; and the module can take timing commands from the ECU, which leads to programmed ignition.

bank.q: Compare distributorless (waste-spark) ignition and direct ignition, and state the advantages of each over a distributor system.
outline: Waste spark: one coil per pair, both plugs fire, one spark wasted
Direct: one coil per plug, fired only on compression
Sensors needed
Losses, interference, accuracy
Service and cost
answer: Distributor system first. One coil serves all cylinders; a rotor and cap share out the high voltage. The rotor gap, cap tracking, long leads and shaft wear cost voltage, cause radio noise and upset the timing.

Waste spark. One double-ended coil per pair of cylinders that are 360° apart (1 & 4 and 2 & 3 on a 1-3-4-2 engine). Each firing sends current out through one plug, through the block and back through the other plug, so the two sparks are in series. One cylinder is at the end of compression and needs most of the voltage; the other is at the end of exhaust and breaks down at a few kilovolts.

Firing rate. Each waste-spark coil fires once per revolution. At 4000 rpm (66.7 rev/s) each coil fires 66.7 times a second, the two coils give 133.3 useful sparks a second, and the firings are 7.5 ms apart.

Direct ignition. One coil per cylinder, on the plug or near it, fired only on its compression stroke, so each coil fires once per 720° and has a whole cycle to recharge. The ECU needs a crank sensor for angle and a cam sensor for phase.

answer.text: Comparison:

answer: Advantages over the distributor, both systems: no rotor gap or cap tracking, so more voltage reaches the plug; less radio interference; no wear, so timing never drifts; no moisture faults in the cap; fewer service items.

Extra advantages of direct ignition: each cylinder can be retarded by its own knock signal; long dwell is always available; misfire can be traced to one coil; and the coil can carry its own igniter (smart coil).

Check: on a 1-3-4-2 engine the firings are at 0° (coil 1 & 4, cylinder 1), 180° (coil 2 & 3, cylinder 3), 360° (coil 1 & 4, cylinder 4) and 540° (coil 2 & 3, cylinder 2): four useful sparks per 720°, as a four-cylinder four-stroke engine needs.

bank.q: Define luminous efficacy and compare tungsten, halogen, HID and LED light sources for automotive use.
outline: Efficacy = lumens out ÷ watts in, lm/W
Principles: incandescence, halogen cycle, gas discharge, electroluminescence
Numbers for each
Start-up, colour, life, cost, drivers
answer: Definition. Luminous efficacy η = Φ ÷ P, the luminous flux Φ in lumens divided by the electrical power P in watts, in lm/W. It tells how much light each watt buys, and so the current and alternator load for a given light output.

Tungsten filament. Current heats a tungsten wire in vacuum to about 2700 K; it glows by incandescence. Most energy leaves as infrared, so η is only 10–15 lm/W, and evaporated tungsten blackens the bulb.

Halogen. Iodine or bromine in the fill carries evaporated tungsten back to the filament (the halogen cycle), so the filament can run at about 3000–3200 K in a small quartz bulb. η ≈ 20–30 lm/W, instant light, warm white, cheap, but hot and short-lived (hundreds of hours).

HID (xenon). A ballast strikes an arc at about 20 kV through xenon and metal salts, then runs it at about 35 W. η ≈ 80–90 lm/W, cool white light, very long life, but it needs a ballast, takes a few seconds to reach full output and, with its very bright beam, needs automatic levelling and headlamp cleaning.

LED. Electrons and holes recombine at a semiconductor junction and emit light; a blue chip with phosphor gives white. η ≈ 90–110 lm/W at the lamp, instant, life of the car, compact so optics can be shaped freely; it needs a constant-current driver and a heat sink, because a hot junction loses output and life.

Other points of comparison. Start-up: filament, halogen and LED light instantly, so they suit flashing lamps and stop lamps; HID does not. Colour: halogen is warm white near 3000 K, HID and LED cooler, closer to daylight. Life: halogen hundreds of hours, HID a few thousand, LED usually the life of the car. Cost: halogen lowest to buy and replace, LED and HID higher. Control: LEDs can be dimmed and switched in segments, which makes matrix beams possible.

answer: Beam patterns. The main beam is a long, symmetrical beam for empty roads. The dipped beam has a sharp asymmetric cut-off: in India (left-hand traffic) it rises on the left to light the kerb and signs and stays low on the right, so oncoming drivers are not dazzled.

Interior lighting. Dome, map, vanity, boot and glovebox lamps. Door switches usually switch the earth side, so opening a door earths the lamp. A body module fades the lamp by PWM; instrument lamps are dimmed the same way.

bank.q: With a labelled sketch, explain the construction and working of an electric horn, and describe a windscreen washer system with wipe-after-wash.
outline: Horn: coil, armature, diaphragm, contacts, tone disc or trumpet, adjusting screw, suppression
Self-interrupting action
Horn relay and its current saving
Washer: reservoir, pump, non-return valve, jets
Wipe-after-wash timer, headlamp washers
answer: Horn construction. A steel diaphragm is clamped at its rim; an iron armature is fixed to its centre and faces the core of an electromagnet coil. A pair of contacts in series with the coil is opened by the armature. A tone disc on the diaphragm (disc horn) or a spiral trumpet (windtone horn) shapes the sound; an adjusting screw sets the contact gap.

Working. Pressing the horn button energises the coil through the contacts. The core pulls the armature, flexing the diaphragm; at the end of the stroke the armature opens the contacts, the current stops, the pull vanishes and the diaphragm springs back, closing the contacts again. The cycle repeats a few hundred times a second, and the diaphragm and disc or trumpet radiate the sound.

Tone and suppression. The contact gap sets the current and so the loudness and tone; a capacitor or resistor across the contacts reduces arcing and radio noise. Cars usually fit a high-note and a low-note horn together for a fuller, more noticeable sound.

answer.text: Horn relay. The horn button carries only the relay coil current; the relay contacts feed the horns on a short, thick wire. For two horns of 4.5 A each and an 80 Ω relay coil on 12 V:

answer: Washer system. A plastic reservoir holds water and screen wash; a small permanent-magnet motor drives a centrifugal pump that draws a few amperes; tubes carry the fluid through a non-return valve, which keeps the line full so fluid reaches the screen at once, to jets or fan nozzles aimed at the wiped area.

Wipe-after-wash. When the driver pulls the washer stalk, the pump runs and the wipers start; after the pump stops, a timer in the relay or body ECU runs the wipers for two or three more strokes so the fluid is spread and then cleared without streaks.

Headlamp washers use a stronger pump and high-pressure telescopic jets, and are required with very bright (HID) dipped beams; rain sensors start the wipers automatically by sensing water on the screen optically.
Check: 0.15 A at the button is within a small switch's rating, while 9.0 A through the button and the steering-wheel contact would burn both, which is why the horn relay is used.

bank.q: A four-cylinder four-stroke engine with contact points runs at 3000 rpm with a dwell angle of 52° (distributor degrees). Calculate the dwell time, then repeat at 6000 rpm and find the coil current and energy at each speed for a coil with L = 8 mH and R = 3.0 Ω on 12 V. State why dwell must be controlled at high speed.
outline: Distributor turns at half engine speed: one revolution takes 40 ms at 3000 rpm
Dwell time = (52/360) × 40 ms = 5.78 ms
At 6000 rpm: 2.89 ms
i = (V/R)(1 − e<sup>−t/τ</sup>), τ = 2.67 ms; E = ½Li²
Fixed angle means less time and energy at speed; electronic dwell control
answer: Convert the dwell angle. On a four-stroke engine the distributor turns at half engine speed. A four-lobe cam gives 360° ÷ 4 = 90° of cam per spark, so 52° is 52 ÷ 90 = 57.8% of each spark interval (104° of crank out of 180°).
Distributor speed at 3000 rpm = 1500 rev/min, so one distributor revolution takes 60 ÷ 1500 = 0.040 s = 40 ms.
Dwell time = (52/360) × 40 ms = 5.78 ms. Check by the spark interval: T<sub>s</sub> = 120 ÷ (3000 × 4) = 10 ms and 0.578 × 10 ms = 5.78 ms.
At 6000 rpm one distributor revolution takes 20 ms, so the dwell time = (52/360) × 20 ms = 2.89 ms, half as long.
Coil current. τ = L/R = 0.008 ÷ 3.0 = 2.67 ms and the final current is 12 ÷ 3.0 = 4.0 A.

answer.text: Current and energy at the break:

answer: Effect. Doubling the speed cuts the energy to 28.0 ÷ 50.2 = 0.56 of its value. Since the available secondary voltage also falls with the current at the break, the voltage reserve shrinks at exactly the time cylinder pressures are high, and the engine misfires at high speed and load.

Why dwell must be controlled. With a fixed angle, dwell time falls in proportion to speed; too little dwell gives a weak spark at high speed, while a long dwell at low speed wastes power and heats the coil. Electronic constant-energy systems therefore set the dwell time (for example 3 ms to reach a limited current) and let the angle grow with speed, holding the energy constant.

Low speed has the opposite problem. At a 500 rpm idle the spark interval is 120 ÷ (500 × 4) = 60 ms and the points stay closed 0.578 × 60 = 34.7 ms, thirteen time constants, so the current sits at the full 4.0 A most of the time. The coil and ballast then dissipate about 12 V × 4.0 A × 0.578 = 27.7 W on average, heating the coil while giving no extra spark energy.
Check: 104° of crank at 3000 rpm lasts 104/360 × 20 ms = 5.78 ms, the same as computed from the distributor, so the two routes agree.

bank.q: A car's two 55 W halogen headlamps are replaced by LED lamps of 20 W each. The lamps are used 2 hours a day. Find the electrical energy saved per year, and the petrol saved if the alternator is 50% efficient, the engine turns fuel into shaft work at 25%, and petrol holds 9.0 kWh per litre at ₹100 per litre. Comment on the result.
outline: Power saved = 2 × (55 − 20) = 70 W
Energy per year = 70 W × 2 h × 365 = 51.1 kWh
Petrol = 408.8 ÷ 9.0 = 45.4 L, worth about ₹4540
Comment: alternator load, lamp life, heat
answer: Power saved: each lamp saves 55 − 20 = 35 W, so two lamps save 70 W.
Daily energy saved: 70 W × 2 h = 140 Wh = 0.14 kWh.
Yearly electrical energy saved: 0.14 × 365 = 51.1 kWh.
Every kilowatt-hour of electricity in a car comes from fuel: the engine drives the alternator. Shaft energy needed = 51.1 ÷ 0.50 = 102.2 kWh; fuel energy = 102.2 ÷ 0.25 = 408.8 kWh.
Petrol saved = 408.8 ÷ 9.0 = 45.4 L per year; money saved = 45.4 × ₹100 = ₹4540 per year.

answer.text: Summary:

answer: Current: the halogen pair draws 110 ÷ 13.2 = 8.33 A, the LED pair 40 ÷ 13.2 = 3.03 A, so the alternator load at night falls by 5.3 A.

Per kilometre: if the 2 hours a day are driven at an average 40 km/h, the car covers 80 km a day or 29 200 km a year, so the saving is 45.4 ÷ 29 200 × 100 = 0.16 L per 100 km, about 3% of a typical small car's 5 L per 100 km.

answer.text: Sensitivity to the assumptions:

answer: Comment: the saving is real but modest per car; it matters more for fleets and for electric cars, where the energy comes from the traction battery. LED lamps also last the life of the car, but they must be designed and approved for the housing, or the beam pattern and cut-off will be wrong and dazzle other drivers.

answer: Sensors. Ride-height sensors, usually a lever on the body linked to the axle or suspension arm turning a Hall or potentiometer sensor, measure the body height at the front and rear axles. Vehicle speed comes over the CAN bus.

Pitch calculation. The ECU takes the difference of the two heights over the wheelbase: tan θ = Δh ÷ b = 0.020 ÷ 2.5 = 0.008, so θ = 0.46°. The whole body, and the lamp with it, tilts nose-up by 0.46°.
Effect on the beam. A slope of 0.008 is 0.8%, so the aim goes from −1.0% to −0.2%. At 25 m the cut-off rises by 25 × 0.008 = 0.20 m, enough to put light into the eyes of oncoming drivers.

Correction. The ECU commands the levelling motors (a stepper motor counted from a reference stop, or a DC motor with a position sensor) to tilt each lamp or reflector down by 0.46°, bringing the aim back to −1.0%. It filters the height signals so bumps do not make the beam twitch; dynamic systems also correct braking dive and acceleration squat.

Braking dive. A dynamic system also reacts to short pitch changes. If hard braking drops the front 15 mm, θ = tan⁻¹(0.015 ÷ 2.5) = 0.34° nose-down and the cut-off at 25 m falls 25 × 0.006 = 0.15 m, shortening the driver's view; a fast motor raises the beam for the duration of the stop. Static systems ignore such short changes and correct only steady load.
Manual levelling. Cheaper cars use a dashboard thumbwheel (positions 0 to 3) that the driver sets for the load; it drives the same motors but relies on the driver remembering to use it.

Fail-safe. If a sensor fails, the lamps move to a low default position and a warning is stored, so the driver still has a legal dipped beam. Very bright dipped beams (HID, many LED) must have automatic levelling by law.
Check: tilting the lamp down by θ = 0.46° lowers the cut-off at 25 m by 25 × tan 0.46° = 0.20 m, exactly cancelling the rise.

bank.q: Describe the challenge-and-response handshake between a transponder key and an immobiliser, how it differs from the rolling code of remote keyless entry, and what the vehicle does when the answer is wrong.
outline: Transponder: chip and coil, no battery, powered at 125 kHz by the barrel coil
Challenge, response computed with a secret key, compared in the immobiliser
Start enable to the engine ECU; cranks but no fuel or spark if wrong
RKE rolling code: counter, window, replay protection
Coding of new keys; why the secret never travels
answer: Parts. The key head holds a transponder: a chip and a small coil, with no battery. A coil antenna round the ignition lock barrel or start button is driven by the immobiliser unit at about 125 kHz. The immobiliser is linked to the engine ECU over the bus or a dedicated wire.

Power and wake-up. When the key is turned or the start button pressed, the antenna sends a 125 kHz field. The transponder coil picks up energy by induction, which powers the chip for a few milliseconds.
Challenge. The immobiliser sends a random number, the challenge, which is different every time.

Response. The chip combines the challenge with its secret key in a cipher and sends back the result by loading its coil (modulating the field). The immobiliser computes the same function with its stored copy of the key and compares. Because the challenge is random and only the result travels, a recording of one exchange cannot be reused, and the secret key itself is never sent.

Start enable. On a match the immobiliser sends a coded start enable to the engine ECU, which itself checks a second code, so swapping the immobiliser box does not help a thief. Only then does the ECU drive the injectors and ignition coils.

Wrong answer. The ECU keeps fuel and spark disabled; the starter usually still cranks, so the engine turns but never fires. The immobiliser lamp flashes, a fault code is stored, and repeated attempts may lock out for a time.

answer.text: Difference from the RKE rolling code:

head: Point
Immobiliser transponder
RKE fob
rows: one-way UHF (315 / 433 MHz), tens of m

answer: Keys and coding. New keys must be taught to the immobiliser with a scan tool and a security code, which stores their identity; lost keys can be deleted so they no longer start the car.

Check: a thief who records an RKE press can open nothing later, because the receiver's counter has moved past it; a thief who records a transponder exchange can start nothing, because the next challenge is different.

answer: Motor. A permanent-magnet DC motor: ferrite magnets give the field and the armature is fed through carbon brushes. A worm and wheel reduce the speed to roughly 40–70 wipes a minute and multiply the torque; a crank and link rods turn rotation into the to-and-fro sweep.

Two speeds. The common brush goes to earth. LOW feeds the brush opposite the common one, with all the armature conductors in series. HIGH feeds a third brush set closer to the common brush, so fewer conductors lie between the brushes in use; they generate less back emf, more current flows and the motor runs faster until the back emf balances the supply.

Park. In OFF the stalk joins the low-speed brush to the park switch, a cam contact in the gearbox. Away from park the cam connects it to +12 V, so the motor keeps running; at park the cam switches it to earth, shorting the armature so the motor brakes dynamically and the blades stop at the bottom of the screen.

Intermittent. An intermittent relay (or the body ECU) closes the motor feed for one wipe, then waits. A capacitor charges through a resistor and fires the relay at about 63% of the supply, so the delay is T = R × C = 100 000 Ω × 100 × 10⁻⁶ F = 10.0 s. A potentiometer on the stalk varies R and so the delay; the park switch completes each wipe.
Washer. The washer pump sprays the screen, and a wipe-after-wash timer runs the wipers for two or three more strokes after the pump stops.

Blade speed. For a 500 mm arm sweeping 120° at 45 wipes a minute, one stroke is 0.500 × 2.094 = 1.047 m and one wipe 2.094 m, so the average tip speed is 0.75 × 2.094 = 1.57 m/s, peaking at about 2.47 m/s mid-sweep.
Protection. A blade frozen to the screen stalls the motor, which then draws a large current; a thermal cut-out in the motor or the ECU's current monitoring switches it off before the armature burns.
Check: with 47 kΩ instead of 100 kΩ the delay becomes 47 000 × 100 × 10⁻⁶ = 4.7 s, so turning the stalk potentiometer down shortens the pause in proportion.

bank.q: Analyse why ignition timing must be advanced as engine speed rises and retarded as load rises, and how knock limits the advance in a programmed ignition system.
outline: Burn takes roughly a fixed time; crank angle per ms grows with speed
Peak pressure should come about 15° after TDC
Light load burns slowly: more advance; full load burns fast and knocks: less
Knock sensor, retard in steps, creep back
Map with corrections
answer: The goal. The charge should burn so that peak cylinder pressure comes about 10–15° after TDC; earlier and the piston is pushed against while still rising, later and the gas expands before it has burned. The spark must be timed to start the burn early enough.

answer.text: Speed. The flame needs roughly the same time from spark to peak pressure, say 2.0 ms, while the crank turns faster. Crank angle covered in 2.0 ms is 2.0 ms × N/60 × 360°:

answer: In real engines turbulence rises with speed and shortens the burn a little, so the advance grows less steeply than this simple model, and flattens at high speed. That is the shape of a centrifugal advance curve.

Load. At light load the throttle is nearly closed: the charge is thin and diluted with left-over exhaust gas, so it burns slowly and needs more advance (vacuum advance). At full load the dense, undiluted charge burns fast, so less advance is needed; extra advance would only raise pressure and temperature before TDC.

Knock. Too much advance at high load makes the unburned end gas ahead of the flame self-ignite. The resulting pressure waves ring the block at a few kilohertz, hammer the piston and overheat it. The best-torque advance is often beyond the knock limit at full load, so the knock limit sets the advance there.

Knock control. A piezoelectric knock sensor on the block picks up the ringing; the ECU looks for it in a window after each spark and, if found, retards that cylinder by a few degrees, then advances again in small steps until knock just returns. The engine thus runs at the knock limit of the fuel actually in the tank and adapts to heat and altitude.

Programmed ignition. The ECU stores the best advance against speed and load in a map, then adds corrections for coolant temperature, cranking and knock. Compared with weights and a diaphragm, the map can follow any shape and never wears.
Effects of too much or too little: too much advance gives knock and high NOx; too little gives low power, high exhaust temperature that can overheat the catalyst, and higher fuel use.
Check: the advance for 1500 rpm (3° BTDC) and 4500 rpm (39° BTDC) differ by 36°, the 54° − 18° extra crank angle covered in the same 2.0 ms.

bank.q: Evaluate the case for fitting LED headlamps instead of halogen lamps on a low-cost Indian car, covering efficacy, current, fuel, heat, beam pattern, legality, life and cost.
outline: Efficacy and current draw; effect on alternator and fuel
Heat: halogen radiates forward, LED conducts back to a heat sink
Beam pattern and cut-off: optics must suit the source
Legality: type approval, colour, aim, levelling
Life, cost, repair, safety; verdict
answer: Frame the question. The car is cheap and sensitive to cost; it is driven on unlit roads with mixed traffic; and the lamp must be legal. The comparison is between a factory LED headlamp and a halogen headlamp, and also the common case of LED bulbs pushed into a halogen housing.

answer.text: Efficacy and current (13.2 V ratings):

answer: Fuel. The 70 W saved over 2 hours a day is 51.1 kWh a year of electricity. With a 50% alternator and 25% engine, that is 408.8 kWh of fuel energy, about 45 L of petrol (at 9.0 kWh/L) or ₹4500 a year at ₹100 per litre. A low-cost car may also fit a smaller alternator.

Light on the road. The LED headlamp gives 33% more flux, and its small source lets designers shape a sharp, even beam; colour near 5500–6000 K looks closer to daylight. Illuminance at a sign 50 m away from a 20 000 cd beam is 20 000 ÷ 50² = 8 lx; raising the beam's intensity by a third raises that to about 10.7 lx.

Heat. A halogen lamp throws most of its waste heat forward as infrared, which also clears frost from the lens. An LED makes less waste heat but it collects at the junction and must be conducted back through a heat sink, often with a fan; in Indian summer temperatures a poor heat sink shortens LED life and dims the output. Lenses may need heating in cold climates.

Beam pattern. A reflector or projector is designed round the exact size and position of its source. An LED bulb in a halogen housing places its light where the filament was not, so the cut-off blurs and light scatters above it into oncoming eyes, even if the lamp looks brighter to the driver. Such retrofits defeat the purpose and are not type-approved.

Legality. Headlamps must be type-approved as a unit: beam pattern, colour (white), intensity limits and aim. Very bright dipped beams also need automatic levelling and headlamp cleaning, which add cost. A factory LED headlamp approved as a unit is legal; a plug-in LED bulb in a halogen lamp is generally not.

Life and cost. An LED module lasts the life of the car, whereas a halogen bulb may need replacing every year or two at low cost. But when an LED headlamp fails, the whole unit (with driver) is usually replaced, at many times the cost of a bulb, and accident repairs cost more.

Safety. Better light helps the driver see pedestrians and cyclists on unlit roads; glare from badly aimed or retrofitted LEDs harms everyone else, and the fast start of LED stop lamps helps following drivers.

answer.text: Weighing up:

head: Factor
Favours
rows: Light quality and beam control (factory unit)

answer: Verdict. For a new design, a factory-approved LED low beam is worth it where the price allows: it saves about ₹4500 of fuel a year in this use, needs no bulb changes and lights the road better. For a cheap car already built with halogen optics, keep halogen bulbs (or change the whole approved lamp unit), because LED bulbs in halogen housings make glare and are not legal.
Check: the LED pair's 3.03 A against the halogen pair's 8.33 A is a 5.3 A cut, the same 70 W ÷ 13.2 V used in the fuel estimate.

bank.q: Analyse how a modern instrument cluster works as a node on the CAN bus and how it measures speed, and what happens when a frame stops arriving.
outline: Microcontroller, CAN transceiver, stepper drivers, display, telltales
Speed from wheel or gearbox pulses: d = C ÷ N, v = 3.6 n d ÷ T
Frames from engine, ABS, body ECUs; update rates; timeout
Default behaviour and fault codes
Contrast with the older directly wired cluster
answer: Hardware. The cluster has a microcontroller with memory, a CAN transceiver, stepper-motor drivers for the needles, an LCD or TFT display, LED telltales and a PWM backlight. A few inputs are wired directly: fuel sender, sometimes the speed sensor, the handbrake and fluid-level switches.

Frames it receives. The engine ECU sends engine speed and coolant temperature; the ABS ECU sends vehicle speed from its wheel sensors; the body module sends lamp, door and indicator states. Each frame has an identifier (which also sets its priority), up to 8 data bytes and a check sum, and is repeated every 10–100 ms depending on how fast it changes.

answer.text: Speed from pulses (wheel sensor, N = 4, C = 1.90 m, gate 0.5 s, true 100 km/h):

answer: Gauge drive. The microcontroller turns each value into a needle angle with a stored curve and steps the motor; it damps the fuel reading so sloshing does not swing the needle, and lights telltales from status bits in the frames.

A frame stops arriving. The cluster watches the time since the last frame of each kind. If, say, the engine-speed frame (normally every 10 ms) is missing for a set timeout, perhaps several hundred milliseconds, it treats the value as invalid rather than showing a frozen number.

Default behaviour: the affected needle drops to zero or the display shows dashes; the matching warning lamp is lit (for example the engine or ABS lamp); a fault code such as "lost communication with engine ECU" is stored in memory; other gauges with good frames carry on. The cluster may sound a chime.

Diagnosis. A technician reads the stored codes through the diagnostic connector, then checks which ECU stopped talking: if several frames from one ECU are missing, the fault is that ECU or its supply; if frames from many ECUs are missing, the bus wiring, its two 120 Ω terminations or a short is suspect.

Contrast with a directly wired cluster: each gauge had its own wire and sender, so a broken wire affected one gauge only and the gauge simply read zero, but the wiring was heavy and the cluster could not store faults.
Check: 29 pulses × 0.475 m = 13.78 m in 0.5 s = 27.55 m/s = 99.2 km/h, 0.8 km/h below the true 100 km/h because the 0.24 part pulse was dropped.

bank.q: Evaluate adaptive front lighting: what it gains the driver, what it costs, and where it can fail. Use a car with a 2.5 m wheelbase and a 20 mm rear drop, and a swivel law of 0.15 × steering-wheel angle capped at 15°, to support your answer.
outline: Functions: levelling, dynamic bending, static cornering, town/country/motorway/adverse-weather, ADB
Numbers: 0.46° pitch, +0.20 m at 25 m; 13.5° and 15° swivel
Gains: see further on bends, less glare
Costs: motors, sensors, ECU, calibration, repair
Failure modes and fail-safe; verdict
answer: What AFS does. It levels the beam for pitch (load, braking, acceleration); swivels it with the steering (dynamic bending light); switches a cornering lamp at junction speed (static cornering light); reshapes the beam for town, country, motorway and wet roads; and, with a camera, keeps the high beam on while blanking other road users (adaptive driving beam).

answer.text: Levelling numbers:
Swivel numbers:

answer: Gains for the driver. On a bend a fixed beam lights the verge; a 13.5° swivel puts light on the lane ahead, so the driver sees an obstacle earlier. A 0.20 m rise at 25 m without levelling is enough to dazzle oncoming drivers, so levelling protects them and keeps the driver's own range from shrinking under braking dive. Motorway light lengthens the beam at speed; adverse-weather light cuts glare from wet roads; ADB lets the driver use the high beam far more of the time.
Gains for others. Less glare for oncoming and leading drivers, the main reason very bright lamps must have automatic levelling.

Costs. Two motors per lamp, ride-height sensors, steering-angle input, an ECU or software in the lamp module, a camera for ADB, more complex type approval, calibration after a wheel-alignment or windscreen change, and expensive repair after a small front-end crash, since the lamp unit holds motors and electronics.

Failure modes. A stuck swivel motor leaves the beam pointing sideways; a drifting height sensor (a bent link after a bump) aims the beam wrongly all the time; a camera that misses a vehicle lets ADB dazzle it; software errors can make the beam twitch over bumps; water in a connector can disable a whole lamp.

Fail-safe design. On any fault the lamps park straight ahead and slightly low, the high-beam assist switches off, and a warning lamp and fault code are set, so the driver always has a legal dipped beam. The swivel command is always capped (15° here) so a wrong steering signal cannot sweep the beam into oncoming traffic.
Checks in service. The technician reads codes, calibrates the height sensors to the unladen car, sets the basic aim (−1.0% here) on a screen, and tests the swivel range against the specification.

Verdict. For a low-cost car, automatic levelling is the most valuable part, because it protects other road users and is required anyway with bright lamps; swivel and ADB give real gains on dark, winding roads but add cost and failure points that mainly suit higher-priced cars. As LED matrix lamps get cheaper, beam shaping in software is replacing moving motors, removing many of the mechanical failures.
Check: tilting the lamp down 0.46° cancels the 0.20 m rise at 25 m (25 × tan 0.46° = 0.20 m), and the swivel law reaches its cap at 15 ÷ 0.15 = 100° of steering-wheel angle.
